podcast.title: "Cubically Contained" Radio Censorship Incident (1996)
podcast.body: An incident occurred in 1996 when an unedited version of the song "Cubically Contained" from the "Smile and Wave" album was broadcast on radio at 5:30 PM, containing explicit profanity. This led to significant repercussions for the program director who played it and generated complaints to the Canadian Broadcast Standards Council. "I played an undated adversion of Cubically Contain on the radio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

podcast.title: 2003 Breakup Due to Addiction
podcast.body: The band broke up in 2003 at Hugh Dillon's behest because he recognized that the band's atmosphere was enabling his addiction, and he feared for his life. Despite the band being their livelihood, manager Bernie Brin and the other members understood the gravity of the situation. "So the band breaks up when? 2003."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

podcast.title: Artistic Control in Modern Recordings
podcast.body: Having learned from past experiences where they questioned management and production decisions, The Headstones now exert full control over their recording process. This autonomy is seen as crucial, with the band believing their newer records, made under their complete direction, are superior and more authentically represent their sound. "That's why now when we make the records, we control everything. And these records to me are the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

podcast.title: Benefit Concert for Randy Kwan's Son
podcast.body: The band played a reunion benefit concert at the Sound Academy for Randy Kwan's son, Hunter, attracting 2500 attendees. This gig was the Headstones' first performance after an eight-year hiatus and a way to honor Randy's memory and support his child. "We played at the Sound Academy, which was like, you know, 2500 people. We hadn't played in eight years or whatever."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

podcast.title: Challenges of Medical Treatment for Addiction
podcast.body: During his initial attempts to get clean and sober, Hugh Dillon tried prescribed drugs like Naltrexone and Antabuse. These medications caused bloating and other issues, leading to comments that made him feel he "looked a lot better when he was shooting heroin," which was a humbling and unhealthy experience. "The trick was for me is to get rid of all of the drugs including the medical drugs that the doctors prescribed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

podcast.title: Chris Ost's Production Contributions
podcast.body: Chris Ost co-produced "Love and Fury" and "Little Army," earning the trust of the band members due to his "ego-less" approach and deep understanding of their musical style, helping them perfect their sound. "By that time we had Chris Ost, he co-producing with us."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

podcast.title: Commitment to Future Touring and Recording
podcast.body: The Headstones are committed to a long future of touring and recording, indicating their ongoing plans and ambition to continue making music. "They plan to be around for a long time, yet, touring and recording."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

podcast.title: Discovery and Signing with MCA
podcast.body: The Headstones were discovered by Cam Carpenter and Tony Wanamaker, who secured them a showcase at the X-ray and Ultra Sound Club. A pivotal moment was the unexpected appearance and endorsement of Gord Downie and Paul Langlois from The Tragically Hip (who were also signed to MCA), which swayed MCA to sign the Headstones despite initial concerns about their "dangerous" image. "I remember when MCA and Cam Carpenter, you know, signed us at ultrasound, they were like, yeah, is it they're a little dangerous yet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

podcast.title: Early 1990s Prime Time Success
podcast.body: Headstones (referred to as "Jail" in transcript) was listed as one of the Canadian bands gaining "prime time" exposure in the early 1990s. "There was Pluto and Jail and Doeboys and Rusty and Sloan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 8: The CanRock Revolution

podcast.title: Early Recklessness with Frankie Venom
podcast.body: In their youth, Hugh Dillon and Frankie Venom engaged in dangerous stunts like bumper hitching on the back of a moving van, which Hugh likened to playing "Jackass" before the show existed. This period illustrates their early bond and daredevil attitudes. "Frank and I are on the back of a van and he's like, let's see how far you can go."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

podcast.title: Early Reputation and Sound
podcast.body: The Headstones were once known as the "scariest band in Canadian music," described as intense, self-destructive, and high-energy. The band's singer, Hugh Dillon, stated that the group's preferred self-description was "furious," highlighting their unique, unpredictable, and ferocious playing style that he likened to a high-energy hockey team. "Once upon a time, the headstones were the scariest band in Canadian music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

podcast.title: Experience with Anhedonia
podcast.body: During his recovery, Hugh Dillon suffered from anhedonia, an inability to experience joy, which compounded the difficulty of his situation alongside his medical treatments and lack of therapy. "So I had a thinkled anodonia. So which means you can't experience joy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

podcast.title: Featured in "In Their Own Words" Series
podcast.body: Headstones was featured in the "In Their Own Words" series, a program for band members to tell their personal history. "Headstones, the Trues..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 1000th Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Gord Lewis's Early Support
podcast.body: Gord Lewis of Teenage Head was a significant fan and supporter of the Headstones, boosting their confidence and believing in their potential. Hugh Dillon recalled a memorable moment sitting in a hotel room with Gord. "Gord Lewis was always such a huge fan that gave us confidence because he was like, you guys can do it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

podcast.title: Hugh Dillon's Recovery Journey
podcast.body: Hugh Dillon's recovery from addiction was a long and arduous process, supported primarily by his wife Midori, manager Bernie Brin, and bandmates Tim White and Trent Carr, who never gave up on him. He underwent multiple rehab and detox programs, eventually reaching a point of honesty that enabled change. "My wife, my family, my wife is the, Midori is the prime mover and all of it because she never, and like these guys, and this is why I go back to the people behind the scenes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

podcast.title: Hugh's Producing Role and Band Dynamics
podcast.body: As a lyricist and singer who took on a producing role, Hugh Dillon often struggled to articulate musical problems, relying on Tim White's ability to "disassemble a song" and Trent Carr's natural, "painter-like" talent, despite the frustration of trying to capture specific takes. "I'm a lyricist and a singer. I don't have the same skill set."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

podcast.title: Intense Touring and "Second Album Syndrome"
podcast.body: Following their debut, The Headstones maintained a grueling touring schedule, playing between 120 and 160 shows a year during the 1990s. This relentless pace led to the "second album syndrome" for "Teeth and Tissue," as songs were often written and recorded hastily on the road, with less time for full development. "I think we've been on the road so much for that pre that record picture of health. And then after it, how many days, I was just, they were doing like 120 shows a year or something like that during the whole 90s, 160 the first, the first year."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

podcast.title: Kingston Origins and Early Formation
podcast.body: The core members originated from Kingston, where they were part of a vibrant music scene that also produced The Tragically Hip. The band's genesis involved a group called "Sean Penn Atenshry" in the mid-1980s, which included Hugh Dillon, Randy Kwan, Mark Gibson, and Frontini, before Trent Carr joined and transformed their sound, leading to The Headstones' formation. "So how the headstones come out of Kingston? What year are we talking about? 89? No, you came from Kingston earlier than that. It was like 80s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

podcast.title: Live-Centric Songwriting Approach
podcast.body: The band's songwriting philosophy prioritizes live performance, ensuring that songs can "stand up live" and genuinely resonate with an audience. This focus dictates what makes it into their setlists and onto new albums, as they believe insincerity would be detected by the crowd or fellow band members. "The songs had in my mind had to stand up live. People had to be able to, you could tell if they uncross their own."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

podcast.title: Opening Act
podcast.body: Big Wreck opened a few shows for the Headstones during a summer in Canada. "we opened a few shows for the headstone and a few shows for the watchman."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Platinum Debut and Studio Challenges
podcast.body: Their debut album, "Picture of Health," achieved platinum status instantly, which was a significant surprise for the band members. They admitted to feeling "totally green" and overwhelmed in the studio environment, and later questioned some of the choices made by producers and managers at that time. "Again, platinum out of the gate. Was that a surprise to you or did you? Oh, very much so a surprise."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

podcast.title: Post-Breakup Hardship for Hugh Dillon
podcast.body: After the Headstones' breakup, Hugh Dillon struggled financially and emotionally, taking jobs like cutting down trees. He felt profound depression and found it difficult to make eye contact with others during this period of adjustment. "I had to go get a job cutting down trees and, you know, watching my hand as I put wood in the wood chipper."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

podcast.title: Producer Brad Nelson's History
podcast.body: Brad Nelson, who produced Pezz's "Wattouche" album, had previously worked with The Headstones and other "bigger Canadian bands" of the time, making his involvement a significant opportunity for Pezz. "But, you know, we had a guy named Brad Nelson who took a chance on us and he had done the headstones and had done all these kind of like, you know, bigger Canadian bands at the time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Randy Kwan as Reunion Catalyst
podcast.body: The Headstones reunited due to the terminal cancer diagnosis of their first bass player, Randy Kwan. Randy, who had previously offered Hugh a place to stay, encouraged Hugh to appreciate the band's legacy and get back together with the other members. "The reunion was this. I had, you know, everyone knew Randy Kwan. Randy was in my typing class."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

podcast.title: Subconscious Noodling Songwriting Method
podcast.body: The band's songwriting often begins with Trent Carr or Tim White "noodling" subconsciously during live performances or jams. Hugh Dillon actively listens for these spontaneous musical ideas, isolating specific notes or riffs that he finds unique and then developing them into full songs, rather than deliberately trying to write "hits." "I'll hear them subconsciously noodle. And that's when I stop everybody and what's that?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

podcast.title: Support from Hamish White
podcast.body: Hugh Dillon received crucial support from Hamish White, an addiction recovery counselor on Young Street. White, who had overcome his own struggles, offered non-judgmental and thoughtful guidance that significantly aided Hugh's journey to sobriety. "I had a you know a addiction recovery counseling a dude named Hamish White up on Young Street who just had been through the ringer himself."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

podcast.title: Tim White's Post-Breakup Career
podcast.body: Following the Headstones' breakup, Tim White continued his career in the recording business, leveraging his expertise as a musician. "Tim's been in the recording business since since I didn't write away right away."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

podcast.title: Trent Carr's Post-Breakup Creative Path
podcast.body: After the band's hiatus, Trent Carr focused on his artistic pursuits and began writing music for film and TV, successfully scoring the film "Giant Sub-Africa," which is available on Netflix. He preferred not to play in another band after the Headstones. "I kind of made it work in that world a little bit and then just kind of kept doing that part of it all kept my toe and being a musician but never tried to play in a band after that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

podcast.title: Unconventional Therapist in Rehab
podcast.body: Hugh Dillon once had an effective therapist in rehab who, despite being "a little odd," proved instrumental in his early recovery, helping him realize the need for honesty. This therapist was later arrested in the parking lot of the rehab facility for robbing banks. "The funny thing is this guy was arrested in the parking lot of the rehab for robbing banks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

podcast.title: Unique Band Dynamic and Talent Respect
podcast.body: The members describe their interpersonal dynamic as jokingly having "no respect" for each other as friends. However, they express profound admiration and shock when they witness each other perform their craft, describing it as a "magic trick" that transforms their perception of their bandmates from mere friends to incredible musicians. "It's funny because I have no respect for you as my friend. You do this magic trick that all of a sudden, whoever that guy, that guy I have all the respect for."

srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

xref.title: Trent Carr's Post-Breakup Creative Path
xref.body: After the band's hiatus, Trent Carr focused on his artistic pursuits and began writing music for film and TV, successfully scoring the film "Giant Sub-Africa," which is available on Netflix. He preferred not to play in another band after the Headstones. "I kind of made it work in that world a little bit and then just kind of kept doing that part of it all kept my toe and being a musician but never tried to play in a band after that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
